title: Rashi's life
hookLine: a winemaker in Troyes who explained the Bible and Talmud

lines: THE SAME VOICE ON THE TALMUD.
cards: A printed page of the Torah, the kind used for study. Look at the column beside the verses: small letters, a slightly different shape from the main text.

Open a page of the Talmud, and there it is again, on the inner margin, close to the spine. The same voice on both, explaining a word here, a sentence there, answering the question a beginner was about to ask.
That voice belongs to a man from a market town in Champagne, in France. He was a scholar. And tradition says he also worked with vines.

teach.b: Rashi is a name from initials: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, Solomon son of Isaac. He was from Troyes.
As a young man he went to study in the Rhine towns, Mainz and Worms, with teachers who had learned from the circle of Rabbeinu Gershom. Then he came home and opened a school.
Tradition says he made his living from vineyards, and readers point to how well his commentary knows pressing grapes and handling wine.
Some historians ask whether that's a memory or a guess; the commentary itself is the evidence people bring.
What he wrote is the point: the plain meaning of the Torah and the Talmud, word by word, for anyone sitting down to learn. Take the first verse.
In the JPS translation: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Rashi's first comment asks a student's question.
If the Torah is a book of commandments, why doesn't it start with the first commandment given to Israel as a people, in Exodus? Why start with creation?
He answers with a teaching of the rabbis: the story of the world comes first, because the whole earth belongs to God, who gives each land to whom God chooses. Notice the habits.

teach.h: PLAIN WORDS, FRENCH WORDS, I DON'T KNOW.
teach.b: He uses the French of his town, written in Hebrew letters, to explain hard words. He says when he doesn't know. And he writes briefly.
His commentary is still printed beside the text: a man who, tradition says, lived by his town's ordinary trade, and made the hardest books readable.

how: Jews studying the weekly Torah portion often read it with Rashi's commentary, and his notes appear on the inner margin of the printed Talmud page.

o: the life of Rashi, a vintner who explained the Torah
the life of a wine merchant who traded on the Rhine
the life of a monk who copied Bibles in Troyes

s: Rashi wrote in the letters printers call Rashi script
printers later used that typeface for his commentary and the name stuck.
Rashi sometimes says he doesn't know
he admits when he doesn't know what a word or verse means.
his first comment asks why the Torah begins with creation
and answers that the story of the world comes first, because the earth belongs to God.

games.q: you are Rashi, starting a commentary on the Torah. what do you write about the very first verse?
o: a student's question: why start with creation and not a commandment?
nothing; the first verse is obvious.
games.why: he asks why the Torah doesn't begin with the first commandment given to Israel, and answers with a teaching of the rabbis.

practice: Think of the work your days are full of, a shift, a commute, a desk, and find one small seam where learning could live: ten minutes before work, a verse on a card in your pocket.
Picture it turning over quietly while you work, the way a grape slowly becomes wine. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for both.

wordCard.voice: Rashi's life. Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki of Troyes: by tradition a vintner, and the teacher whose commentary sits beside the Torah and the Talmud. Today's word.
